purpose: An architecture document says how the product delivers its UX, as a framework and principles. The framework is the product's parts and how they relate. Each principle comes with its reason, so a builder applies it to a case it did not foresee. The framework and the principles hold as long as the UX stays, whatever the implementation. Whoever builds or changes the product, a person or an AI, derives each part's specification from the document and implements it. Because every builder works from the same framework and principles, they do not hesitate over each part, and every part is made on the same thinking. So the product stays readable, maintainable and resilient to change.

format.skeleton:
# <Product name> architecture

<How the product delivers its UX, in a sentence or two, with a link to the UX>

## Principles

<A link to the principles of the architecture this one is built on, where there is one>

### <A short name for the principle>

<The rule every part is built by, in a sentence>

<Its reason: what the rule is there for, and what goes wrong for the user or the builder without it>

## User stories

- As <the user>, I want <one way they use the product at its edge, such as a command they run>. Carries <the UX's scenarios, or their steps, that rest on it>.

## Architecture

### Logical view

#### Components

<One SVG figure in the notation of a C4 component diagram: a box for each role the user stories need and each store of data, holding its name and a tag of its type and technology, such as "[agent · Claude prompt]" or "[module · Python]", and no sentence; the box's shape saying whether an AI or code runs it; an arrow from each to the one it acts on, labelled with what it does and the data it hands on, named as in the data model, and with the protocol where it matters, such as "[HTTPS/JSON]"; a legend of the shapes and the tags; the boxes placed so the arrows run in the order they act and cross none>

- <What a role alone is responsible for that no arrow shows>
- <A choice the figure shows that the reader would question, such as a technology, with why it was made over the other way>

#### Data model

<One SVG figure in the notation of an ER diagram: a box for each data the roles pass or keep, holding its name alone; a line between two data for each relation between them, labelled with the relation's name, its ends drawn in crow's-foot notation for its cardinality, such as one to many>

#### Sequences

<For each user story, a UML sequence diagram in Mermaid: a participant for the user, for each role the story reaches, named as in Components, and for each thing outside the product it reaches; a message for each step, labelled in a few words with what one does and the data handed on, named as in the data model>

- <A choice the diagrams show that the reader would question, with why it was made over the other way>

### Physical view

#### Deployment

<One SVG figure in the notation of a C4 deployment diagram: an outer box for each execution environment, such as Cloud Run, Claude Code, the user's repository or CI, with its technology tag; inside it a box for each deployment unit, such as an app or a container, named with its technology tag, holding by their names, as in Components, the roles that run in it and the data kept in it; a box for each thing outside the product they depend on, with an arrow labelled with what is used>

- <How the product is started>
- <A choice the figure shows that the reader would question, such as a technology, with why it was made over the other way>

#### Directory structure

```text
<A tree of the folders and files of the product; each line that holds a role or a data names it as in Components, with its technology tag>
```

## Test

<A link to the project's shared test rules, where it has them; what follows says only what differs from them>

| Deployment unit | Unit | Integration | End-to-end |
|---|---|---|---|
| <Each deployment unit, named as in Deployment with its technology tag> | <Tool · weight, such as ●●● or ●●○ · what it checks, in a few words> | <The same> | <The same, or ▨ and a footnote mark where the cell is empty> |

[^1]: <Why the cell is empty>

- <Each deployment unit left out because every cell of its row would be empty, with why>
- Unit tests: <what they make real and what they fake>. Pass: <all pass; line and branch coverage at least a threshold; at the heaviest weight, also property tests pass and the mutation score is at least a threshold>
- Prompt trials: <what they make real and what they fake>. Pass: <N runs for each fixed input, and how many must meet the expectation>
- Integration tests: <what they make real and what they fake>. Pass: <the criteria>
- End-to-end tests: <what they make real and what they fake>. Pass: <the criteria>
- <Each deployment unit's weight, with what a failure of it would cost the user>
- <A choice the table shows that the reader would question, such as a tool, with why it was made over the other way>

parts.what: The title, and the sentence or two under it, with a link to the UX.
parts.why: The builder holds the one idea of how the product delivers its UX before reading the rest, and builds each part as a piece of it.

parts.what: One subsection for each principle, holding the rule and its reason, after a link to the principles of the architecture this one is built on, where there is one.
parts.why: The builder decides each detail by the rules every part is built by, and decides a case no rule names from a rule's reason.

parts.what: A list under its heading, one item for each story, each naming the UX's scenarios or steps that rest on it.
parts.why: The builder sees each way the user uses the product at its edge, and draws the roles and the data from them.

parts.what: The figure under Components, an SVG file beside the document drawn by hand in the notation of a C4 component diagram: each box a role's or a store's name and a tag of its type and technology, its shape saying whether an AI or code runs it, each arrow what one does to another with the data and the protocol where it matters, and a legend.
parts.why: The builder sees, at a glance, the roles to build, what each is made with, and what each does to which.

parts.what: The first items of the list under Components: what a role alone is responsible for that no arrow shows.
parts.why: The builder finds the rest of a role's responsibility next to the figure, without the box being read as text.

parts.what: The items of the lists under Components, Sequences, Deployment and Test that give a choice the reader would question, such as a technology or a tool, with why.
parts.why: The builder finds why a choice they question was made, next to the figure that shows it.

parts.what: The figure under Data model, an SVG file beside the document drawn by hand in the notation of an ER diagram: each box a data's name, each line a relation's name with its cardinality.
parts.why: The builders of the role that writes a data and of the role that reads it take each relation, and how many of each it joins, the same way.

parts.what: The UML sequence diagrams in Mermaid under Sequences, one for each user story; a sequence has one layout, its order down the page, so Mermaid draws it from text.
parts.why: The builder follows each story through the roles, in order, with the data each hands on.

parts.what: The figure under Deployment, an SVG file beside the document drawn by hand in the notation of a C4 deployment diagram: each outer box an execution environment, holding the deployment units, each with its technology tag and the roles and data in it; and the list under it, of how the product is started and of choices.
parts.why: The builder puts each role and each data in the deployment unit and the environment where it runs or is kept, and starts the product.

parts.what: The tree under Directory structure, in text, as the files lie, each line that holds a role or a data naming it as in Components with its technology tag.
parts.why: The builder finds the one place to make or change each role and each data.

parts.what: The table under Test: a row for each deployment unit, a column for each test type from narrow scope to wide, unit, integration and end-to-end; each cell a tool, a weight and what it checks in a few words, an empty cell hatched with a footnote; and the note of the units left out.
parts.why: The builder sees at a glance which unit is tested by which type of test, how heavily and with what, and why a cell is empty.

parts.what: The lines under the table: for each test type, including prompt trials, what it makes real, what it fakes and when it passes; each unit's weight with what a failure costs the user; and a link to the project's shared test rules, with only what differs written here.
parts.why: The builder writes each test with the right neighbours real or faked, knows when the tests pass, and knows why a unit is tested as heavily as it is.

checklist.what: When a colleague asks "How does the product deliver its UX?", can the builder answer in a sentence or two?
checklist.why: If yes, the builder holds the one idea every part comes from, and builds each part as a piece of it, so the parts fit together as one design. The opening links the UX, so the builder knows which experience the parts must deliver. If no, the builder meets the parts one by one, cannot tell which part carries the idea, and builds each on its own thinking.

examples.fails: RoomBook is built on a modern, scalable cloud architecture.
examples.passes: RoomBook reads the meeting a worker describes, matches it to the rooms whose seats and equipment fit, and asks the office calendar which of them are free, so the worker is offered only rooms that fit. The UX it delivers is in ux.md.

checklist.what: When the builder meets a case no principle names, can they decide it by naming the principle whose reason settles it?
checklist.why: If yes, the builder decides a case the document did not foresee as its writer would have, because each principle says what it is there for. A principle is a rule every part is built by; a means, such as a language or a tool, is not one. If no, a rule with no reason is either stretched to a case it was not meant for or ignored where it was, and the builder asks, or guesses.

examples.fails: Principle: RoomBook does not read calendars. (A builder adding a reminder email cannot tell whether it may read the attendees' free times to pick when to send it.)
examples.passes: Principle: RoomBook reads only whether a room is free, never what is in a person's calendar. Reason: staff let RoomBook in on that promise alone, and one look into a person's meetings breaks it for everyone. (The builder sends the reminder a day before the meeting, without reading anyone's calendar.)

checklist.what: For each step of each of the UX's scenarios, can the builder tell which entry of the product the user uses for it, such as a command they run?
checklist.why: If yes, the builder sees that the roles, the parts that act, drawn from these ways of use deliver every step of the UX. These ways of use are the document's user stories. If no, a step no user story carries is built by guess. A user story for a step inside the product adds roles without the user doing more, and one named by a technology rather than by what the user does must be written again when the technology changes.

A story for a step inside the product adds components without the user doing more, and a story named by a technology rather than by what the user does must be made again when the technology changes."

examples.fails: As the server, I want to cache each room's free times. (The worker never does this, and no story carries the UX's step where the worker finds a room that fits.)
examples.passes: As an office worker, I want to describe my meeting and get the rooms that fit it. Carries O1, steps 1-2. As an office worker, I want to book one of them and find it in my calendar. Carries O1, steps 3-4.

checklist.what: When the builder starts on a role, can they build it without choosing for themselves what it is made with: an AI or code, and which technology?
checklist.why: If yes, every role of a kind is made the same way, and the builder starts at once. The box's shape says whether an AI or code runs the role, its tag names its type and technology, and a technology the builder would question has its reason under the figure. Code is for what a machine can decide the same way every time, and an AI for what needs a reader. If no, a role meant for code is left to an AI and decides differently from run to run, or each builder picks their own language, and a role relies on what the users do not have.

checklist.what: When the builder asks "Which role decides this?" of anything the UX needs, can they point to exactly one role?
checklist.why: If yes, each thing is decided once, in one role, and a change to it is made in that role alone. A role's responsibility shows in what it does to the others, and the list holds what no arrow carries. Each role acts in a user story, and is split from the others by a responsibility of its own, or by a constraint or a principle the document names, such as work run in parallel or what the platform allows. If no, roles cut by function, by stage of processing or to fit a technology grow with each function and leave a thing decided in two roles or in none, so two builders decide it two ways, or one decides it by guess.
grounds: plugins/rn/checklists/product/architecture.md:141-148: "Is each role one that acts in a user story" and "components cut by function or by stage of processing grow with each function, and scatter what one thing knows among them" and "leaves one responsibility decided in two places."

plugins/rn/checklists/product/architecture.md:18-20: "Whoever makes the architecture cuts no component by function or by stage of processing, nor to fit a technology, and chooses a technology for each component after."

checklist.what: When the builder doubts a choice the document makes, such as a technology, can they tell why it was made over the other way?
checklist.why: If yes, the builder keeps the choice or changes it knowing what it was for, since its reason stands next to the figure or the table that shows it. If no, a later builder has two ways only: to keep the choice blindly, or to change it blindly and undo what it was for.

checklist.what: When one builder makes the role that writes a data and another makes the role that reads it, do they take the way the data join the same way?
checklist.why: If yes, the two roles work together the first time they meet, as each relation is drawn once, named, with how many of one go with one of the other (its cardinality) at its ends, and both read it. The figure names each data alone: a data's contents, such as its fields, are decided where the data is built, and its schema's file shows in the directory structure. If no, a relation no figure draws, or one drawn without how many it joins, is made one way by the role that writes it and read another way by the role that reads it, and the fault shows only when the two run together.

checklist.what: When the builder traces one user story, one way the user uses the product, can they follow it from the first role it reaches to its end, with the data each role hands on?
checklist.why: If yes, the builder sees that the roles together carry each story, not only each its own share, and builds each role knowing which steps it carries. Roles and data keep the names Components and the data model give them, so each step is read against those figures. If no, a role found missing only when its story is built is then added to whichever role is nearest, by guess, and a data the builder cannot follow from the role that makes it to the role that uses it is made in one form and read in another.

examples.fails: Browser ->> Server: request; Server -->> Browser: response. (The step where the worker finds the booking in their calendar is carried by no role, so the builder of the Booking page adds a calendar call of its own.)
examples.passes: Worker ->> Booking page: books a room; Booking page ->> Booking API: booking; Booking API ->> Calendar link: booking; Calendar link ->> Google Workspace: puts the booking on the room's and the worker's calendars; Booking API -->> Booking page: booking confirmed.

checklist.what: When the builder sets up and starts the product, can they put each role and each data where it runs or is kept, without asking anyone?
checklist.why: If yes, the builder knows where each role runs, and so what it can reach and when a change to it reaches the user, and where each data is kept, and so who can read it and whether it outlives a run. Each place the product runs, such as a container, sits in an outer box of its environment, such as Cloud Run, holding the roles that run in it and the data kept in it, each tagged with its technology, so the builder sets up what each needs. The list under the figure says how the product is started, and each thing outside the product the roles depend on is drawn, as it is where the product breaks for the user first. If no, the builder places a role or a data by guess, and finds what it cannot reach only once it runs.

checklist.what: When the builder makes or changes a role or a data, can they put its files in the one place they belong, without asking anyone?
checklist.why: If yes, the builder makes each role and each data where it is kept, and the place tells who owns it. If no, a role kept in no place is put where the builder guesses, and one kept in two places is made twice and drifts.

checklist.what: When a colleague asks "Is anything in this product left untested?", can the builder answer, for each place the product runs, such as the Booking API container, which types of test from unit to end-to-end cover it, and why a type is missing where it is?
checklist.why: If yes, the builder sees that every place the product runs is tested from narrow scope to wide, or why not: unit tests take the roles inside a place one at a time, an AI part by prompt trials; integration tests join the place to its real neighbours; end-to-end tests run on the whole alone. A row of Test's table is such a place, named as in Deployment, and an empty cell has its reason in a footnote, so the builder knows what each test runs against. If no, a place with no row, or an empty cell with no reason, goes untested unseen, and many narrow tests with no wide one pass while a user story fails.

Winters, Manshreck and Wright, Software Engineering at Google, ch. 11 "Testing Overview": "Scope refers to the specific code paths we are verifying."

checklist.what: When the builder writes a test of one type, such as an integration test, can they write it without deciding for themselves what to make real and what to fake?
checklist.why: If yes, every test of a type stands, by the line for its type under Test's table, on the same ground, so a failing test points to the part it is about: a unit test fakes the part's neighbours, a prompt trial runs the real prompt and model on a fixed input, an integration test makes real the neighbours of the place it tests. If no, one builder's integration test fakes the database and another's does not, so a fault passes one and the two tests disagree on what broke.

checklist.what: When the builder has run the tests of a place the product runs, can they judge whether it passes without setting the bar themselves?
checklist.why: If yes, every builder stops at the same bar: all tests pass, line and branch coverage reach their threshold, the heaviest weight also passes property tests and reaches its mutation score, and a prompt trial meets its expectation in the given share of runs on each fixed input. If no, each builder sets their own bar, so a place passes for one and fails for another, and a prompt that met its expectation once is taken as working, though an AI's output varies from run to run.

examples.fails: Unit tests: good coverage. Prompt trials: the Meeting reader reads a sample meeting.
examples.passes: Unit tests: all pass; line and branch coverage at least 90%; at ●●●, property tests pass and the mutation score is at least 95%. Prompt trials: 10 runs for each fixed input, at least 9 give the expected Meeting request.

checklist.what: When a colleague asks "Why is this place the product runs tested so heavily, and that one so lightly?", can the builder answer by what a failure of each would cost the user?
checklist.why: If yes, each place gets the checks its failure is worth, weighed once for this product, and what the project's shared rules settle is linked rather than weighed again. If no, a weight given every product alike gives a small tool the checks of a large one, or a costly place too few, and a ground such as "a checklist asks it" is one the builder cannot weigh against the user.

examples.passes: Booking API container ●●●: a wrong match puts a six-person review in a four-seat room. Booking page app ●○○: a fault in it shows on the screen at once.

checklist.what: When two builders, each making a different role, meet the same detail the document does not settle, do they decide it the same way by the same principle?
checklist.why: If yes, every role is made on the same thinking, and the user meets one product, not one for each builder. The principles cover the decisions that come up in every role, such as what to do when something outside the product does not answer, and each is plain enough that two builders read it alike. If no, a recurring decision with no principle, or a principle each reads their own way, such as "keep it simple", is decided differently in each role, and the user meets two behaviours where they expect one.

Brooks, The Mythical Man-Month (1975): "I will contend that conceptual integrity is the most important consideration in system design."

examples.fails: No principle says what to do when Google Workspace does not answer. (The builder of the Room matcher offers every room that fits; the builder of the Booking page shows an error. The worker gets a list one day and an error the next.)
examples.passes: Principle: RoomBook never offers a room it has not seen free. Reason: a room offered and then found taken spoils the meeting it was booked for. (Both builders show that rooms cannot be checked now, and offer none.)

checklist.what: When the builder changes how a role works inside, such as its steps, its behaviour in one case or a data's fields, while the UX and the principles stay, does every line of the document still hold?
checklist.why: If yes, the builder chooses the best way to build each role and changes it freely, and the document stays true for every builder after them. How a role behaves in each case is decided where it is built, in its tests if it is code and in its steps if an AI runs it, and a data's fields are decided where the data is built. A technology is a choice the document makes, shown as a tag with its reason, so changing one is a change of the document's choice, made with a new reason. If no, a line that holds such a detail, such as a count, a value or a role's steps, or a technology named in prose, is decided again where the role is built, drifts from it, and is followed by the next builder as if it still held.
grounds: plugins/rn/checklists/product/architecture.md:9-12: "How a part behaves in each case is decided where the part is built: in its tests if it is code, and in its steps if an AI runs it. The contents of each data, such as its fields, are decided where the data is built too".

plugins/rn/checklists/product/architecture.md:190-191: "a behavior in one case, a count, a value, a data's fields or a list of what a part does step by step is decided again where the part is built and drifts from it."
Ubl, "Design Docs at Google": "A clear indicator that a doc might not be necessary are design docs that are really implementation manuals."

examples.fails: Under Components: "The Room matcher reads rooms with one SQL join, caches the result for five minutes, and retries Google Workspace three times." (Moving the cache or the retry into the Calendar link leaves these lines untrue.)
examples.passes: Under Components: "The Room matcher offers a room only when it is free for the whole meeting." The Room matcher's queries, caching and retries change, and the line still holds.

checklist.what: When the builder asks of any role, line or principle "Why is this here?", can they answer by a step of the UX or by a principle's reason?
checklist.why: If yes, the document changes only when the UX or a principle changes, and the builder who makes such a change finds from it every role and line the change reaches. They keep what still has its reason and remove what has lost it. If no, a choice with no reason is neither kept nor removed with confidence: a later builder keeps it blindly, or changes it blindly and undoes what it was for.
grounds: Nygard, "Documenting Architecture Decisions" (2011): without the motivation, a new team member can only "Blindly accept the decision." or "Blindly change it."
arc42, section 9 "Architecture Decisions": "Stakeholders of your system should be able to comprehend and retrace your decisions."

examples.fails: A role, Notification hub, that no user story reaches and no principle asks for. (A builder cannot tell whether removing it breaks anything.)
examples.passes: The Calendar link is the only role that talks to Google Workspace, by the principle "one role speaks to each outside service", whose reason is that a change on Google's side then reaches one role alone.
